Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
The storm arrived without warning on a humid August night. Thao, a third-generation Vietnamese-American who had lived in this coastal town for twenty years, was sleeping when the wind first tore through the eaves, followed by the sharp, unpredictable crack of a pine snapping against the roof. When the windows gave way, the glass hit the floor in a sudden, deafening scatter. Water surged through the hallway, knocking furniture aside, and the house groaned as the foundation shifted. Thao dragged her husband toward the higher shelves, listening to the relentless roar and the sharp clatter of debris racing across the floor. The violence was never gradual; it arrived in sudden, deafening bursts that left no time to brace herself. In the weeks that followed, Thao’s body remained tuned to that same suddenness. She would lie in bed, staring at the ceiling, certain she needed to stay awake for the noise. When her husband finally drifted off, she pulled the covers to her chin, ready for the next sharp crack or thud. What frightened her most was the darkness itself; night had become a place where she found it harder to feel safe than during the day. The memory of the event never arrived as a straight narrative. Instead, fragments would force their way into her mind when she was folding laundry or measuring ingredients for dinner: a sudden image of a shattered pane, the sharp sound of water hitting hardwood, the feeling of a floor tilting beneath her boots. Each piece would surge up on its own, bringing such a heavy wave of emotion that she would have to step away from the counter or drop her phone, certain she could not push through the feeling. Thao’s closing shifts at the fast food restaurant on the edge of town became a place of constant navigation. She spent her hours wiping down stainless steel counters and folding cardboard in the dim, humming kitchen. One Tuesday, a delivery truck reversed past the drive-thru with a sharp, unexpected beep that echoed off the brick exterior. Thao froze, her hands hovering over a stack of napkins, her breath catching as the sound sliced through the room. She was certain the noise was the same type of sudden threat that had come before. Over the following months, she began requesting only the daytime schedule. The habit solidified as her supervisor noted the reduced hours on her timesheet, and she quietly took on weekend stock work instead. At home, the change settled into her marriage. Thao stopped sleeping in her marital bed, choosing instead the stiff sofa in the living room, telling her husband she only needed a quiet corner to rest. She had come to believe that she could not stop bad things from happening, that the world was built to surprise her with disaster no matter how carefully she planned. Over time, she felt she would never be able to feel normal emotions again, as though the storm had sealed her heart behind glass. The sense that she no longer belonged anywhere settled heavily on her shoulders; she felt like a guest in her own neighborhood, watching others laugh in their yards while she measured every gust of wind. It was the accumulated weight of those long nights and the quiet distance at the dinner table that finally brought Thao to the clinic. She sat across from the intake counselor now, hands folded tightly in her lap, hoping someone could help her untangle the fear that had taken root. What she wanted most was simply to sleep through the night without listening for a storm, and to walk past the restaurant without her shoulders tensing at the sound of a closing door. She was willing to sit with the memories, she said, if she could finally stop feeling like the ground was always about to give way.
